To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) exclusive Higgs production is a very promising process for the LHC; 2) the Higgs mass range where this process is accessible at the LHC is 120 GeV < m_H < 140 GeV (at 14 TeV); 3) the Higgs production rate is very sensitive to the Higgs mass, and the cross section is large, 0.2-1 fb, in the mass range 130-140 GeV;
the exclusive Higgs production cross section is very small, and the exclusive cross section for Higgs production in association with a photon is also small.

the LHC will be able to detect exclusive Higgs production, with the rate of 0.1-0.3 pb, depending on the value of the Higgs width and the Higgs mass, if it is in the range of 120-150 GeV; the Tevatron will be able to observe exclusive Higgs production if it is in a narrow mass range around 130 GeV, with the rate in that range being 0.2 pb.

the following issues.
the study of the diffractive production of Higgs bosons and of other particles in hadron-hadron collisions.
the production of Higgs bosons in association with jets, and the production of two Higgs bosons.

, although the exclusive Higgs production cross-sections at the LHC are very small, the Higgs signal is not completely lost in the background.

exclusive Higgs production in the gluon fusion channel is not possible at the LHC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Higgs boson can be detected through diffractive processes at the LHC with a cross section which is of order of 1fb.

the LHC has a very good chance of discovering the Higgs boson via exclusive production in the 8 TeV run, even if the Higgs is light.
